theme: The word of life; walking in light; the antichrists
readingInstruction: Read 1 John 1:1-2:29. John writes as an eyewitness of Jesus and gives tests by which his readers can know that they have eternal life. Notice the repeated themes of light and darkness, truth and lies, and love and hate.
settingTheScene: The apostle John, the last living eyewitness, wrote this letter in his old age, probably from Ephesus in the 80s or 90s AD. A group had left the church (2:19), claiming a higher knowledge, denying that Jesus had come in the flesh, and living as though sin did not matter. John writes to assure true believers and expose the counterfeit. There is no formal greeting; he begins like a sermon. His message is simple and deep: the God who is light and love has come to us in Jesus, and those who know him walk in the light and love one another.
observation: “That which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands” (1:1).
“God is light, and in him is no darkness at all” (1:5).
“The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1:7).
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1:9).
“We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (2:1).
“He is the propitiation for our sins” (2:2).
“Do not love the world or the things in the world” (2:15).
“They went out from us, but they were not of us” (2:19).
interpretation:
John begins by insisting that the Word of life was heard, seen, and touched. The Christian faith is not a myth or an idea but the testimony of those who handled the incarnate Son. The purpose of this witness is fellowship: “that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.” He writes “that our joy may be complete.”

The message is this: “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.” Then John gives three false claims and three true responses. If we claim fellowship with him while walking in darkness, we lie. But “if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.” If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves. But “if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” He is faithful (he keeps his promises) and just (the price was paid by Christ). If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar. Walking in the light does not mean sinless perfection; it means honest confession.

Chapter 2 opens tenderly. “My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.” Propitiation means the sacrifice that turns aside God’s wrath. Christ is both the advocate who pleads for us and the sacrifice that makes the plea valid. The phrase “the whole world” has been understood in different ways: that Christ’s sacrifice is sufficient for all and sincerely offered to all, or (as many Reformed interpreters hold) that it is for people from every nation and not for Jews only. Either way, the focus is on the sufficiency and reach of his work.

The tests of knowing God are obedience and love. “And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments.” Whoever says he abides in him ought to walk as he walked. The old commandment is a new commandment that is true in Christ: whoever loves his brother abides in the light; whoever hates his brother is in darkness. John then addresses children, fathers, and young men with a message of forgiveness, knowledge of him who is from the beginning, and victory over the evil one.

The second warning is against the world: “Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the world, the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride in possessions, is not from the Father but is from the world. And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever.”

The final section warns about antichrists. “Children, it is the last hour, and as you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come.” The last hour began with Christ’s first coming. The antichrists denied that Jesus is the Christ. “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But they went out, so that it might become plain that they all are not of us.” Departure revealed their true nature. By contrast, believers have an anointing from the Holy One and know the truth. John exhorts: “And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.”
connection: John 1:1-14 and Luke 24:39 relate to the eyewitness testimony. Psalm 32:1-5 and Proverbs 28:13 speak of confession. Romans 3:25 and Hebrews 2:17 use propitiation language. Romans 8:34 and Hebrews 7:25 describe Christ’s intercession. John 13:34-35 gives the new commandment. Genesis 3:6 echoes the three desires in 2:16. Matthew 24:24 and 2 Thessalonians 2 speak of antichrists. John 14:26 and 16:13 promise the Spirit as teacher. Hebrews 6:4-6 and 10:26-31 speak of falling away. John 6:66-69 shows disciples who left Jesus.
application:
Confess a specific sin today. Believe the promise of 1:9 and receive the forgiveness: he is faithful and just.

When you sin this week, remember you have an advocate. Run to him, not away.

Examine your loves. What “world” desire has been competing with the love of the Father?
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he is light, and ask him to help you walk in it.
Confess your sin and thank him for forgiving it.
Ask him to keep you from loving the world.
